---
title: "Exponential (λ = 1)"
subtitle: "A strongly right-skewed population: think waiting times"
---

```{r}
#| label: simulate
#| code-summary: "Show the simulation code"
source("../R/clt_functions.R")

rgen  <- function(n) rexp(n, rate = 1)   # one sample of size n
mu    <- 1                               # population mean
sigma <- 1                               # population SD
pop_skew <- 2                            # population skewness
pop_kurt <- 6                            # population excess kurtosis

# Stage 1: a coarse grid of sample sizes. Stage 2 (automatic): every n
# between the last coarse n that failed and the first one that passed.
coarse <- c(1, 2, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 45, 60, 80, 100, 150, 200,
            300, 400, 450, 500, 600, 750, 1000)
exper <- run_with_refinement(rgen, coarse, mu, sigma)

res    <- exper$results
n_main <- smallest_normal_n(res)
n_std  <- n_by_standard(res)
at     <- function(k) res[res$n == k, ]
n_first <- min(res$n[res$normal_enough])   # first n that passes at all

save_results(res, "exponential")
save_summary(res, "Exponential(1)", n_main, prediction = "45",
             key_note = "Skewness is the bottleneck; theory predicts (2/0.25)^2 = 64")
```

::: {.answer-box}
<span class="big">n = `r n_main`</span> under my main standard
(strict standard: ≈ `r n_std[["strict"]]` · lenient standard: ≈ `r n_std[["lenient"]]` · my prediction: 45)
:::

## 1. What population am I sampling from?

The exponential distribution describes waiting times: the time until the next customer arrives,
the next call comes in, or a machine fails. Most waits are short, but occasionally a wait is very long,
which gives the distribution a long right tail.

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Mean μ | 1 |
| Standard deviation σ | 1 |
| Skewness | 2 (strong right skew) |
| Excess kurtosis | 6 (heavy right tail) |
| Theoretical SE of the mean | σ/√n = 1/√n |

```{r}
#| label: fig-population
#| fig-cap: "The population itself: 100,000 draws from Exponential(1) with the true density."
#| fig-height: 4
set.seed(student_id)
style_par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
x <- rexp(100000, rate = 1)
hist(x[x < 8], breaks = 60, freq = FALSE, col = adjustcolor(pal$bars, 0.75),
     border = "white", main = "", xlab = "Waiting time", ylab = "Density")
curve(dexp(x, 1), add = TRUE, col = pal$curve, lwd = 2.2)
```

## 2. What did I expect before running the simulation?

> I based my prediction on a pilot run at n = 1, 15 and 20. The skewness of the sample means dropped
> from 0.52 at n = 15 to 0.45 at n = 20, and I extrapolated that it would reach my 0.25 limit around
> **n = 45**. From the river-length example (see [Real data](06_real_world_data.qmd)) I already
> expected that n = 30 would not be enough for a strongly skewed population.

## 3. Which sample sizes did I investigate?

I used the same two-stage search for every population:

1. **Coarse grid:** n = `r paste(coarse, collapse = ", ")`, wide enough to cover both the main
   and the strict standard.
2. **Refinement:** every n from `r min(exper$refined)` to `r max(exper$refined)`, the gap
   between the last coarse n that failed and the first one that passed.

For every n I simulated **B = 100,000** sample means with seed `r student_id`. B only controls how
precisely each sample size is measured; it is not the sample size.

## 4. Results

### The four checks as n grows

```{r}
#| label: fig-convergence
#| fig-cap: "The four numerical checks. Shaded band = pass zone; green = pass, red = fail. Orange curves are the theoretical values 2/√n and 6/n; the dotted line is the chosen n."
#| fig-height: 6.5
plot_convergence(res, chosen_n = n_main, theory_skew = pop_skew, theory_kurt = pop_kurt)
```

Skewness is clearly the bottleneck here. Excess kurtosis passes already at
n = `r first_stable_n(res$n, res$kurt_ok)`,
but the skewness falls slowly, following the theoretical curve 2/√n almost exactly.
The Q-Q correlation and the tail check cross their limits at about the same point as the skewness,
which is what my calibration in [Method](../methods.qmd) was designed to do.

### Histograms of the sample means

```{r}
#| label: fig-hist
#| fig-cap: "Sampling distribution of the mean (bars) and the normal curve predicted by the CLT (red)."
#| fig-height: 6
n_show <- c(1, 5, 30, 45, n_main, 300)
plot_hist_grid(exper, n_show, mu, sigma)
```

### Normal Q-Q plots

```{r}
#| label: fig-qq
#| fig-cap: "Normal Q-Q plots. The upward bend at the right end is the leftover right skew."
#| fig-height: 6
plot_qq_grid(exper, n_show)
```

### Simulation vs. theory

```{r}
#| label: fig-se
#| fig-cap: "The SD of the simulated means (dots) follows σ/√n (line) at every n."
#| fig-height: 4.2
plot_se_check(res)
```

Across all `r nrow(res)` sample sizes, the simulated mean stayed within
`r f4(max(abs(res$sim_mean - mu)))` of μ = 1, and the ratio of simulated SE to σ/√n stayed between
`r f3(min(res$se_ratio))` and `r f3(max(res$se_ratio))`. The formula for the standard error holds at
every n, even at n = 1 where the shape is far from normal. **The SE is right long before the shape is.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

## 5. When did the sampling distribution become approximately normal?

$$\boxed{n = `r n_main`}$$

```{r}
#| label: tbl-standards
#| echo: false
standards_table(res)
```

## 6. Why did I choose that value?

- At **n = `r n_main`** all four checks pass: skewness `r f3(at(n_main)$skewness)`,
  excess kurtosis `r f3(at(n_main)$ex_kurtosis)`, Q-Q correlation `r f4(at(n_main)$qq_cor)`,
  and tails of `r pct(at(n_main)$lower_tail, 2)` / `r pct(at(n_main)$upper_tail, 2)`.
  **Every larger n I tested also passes.**
- `r flip_text(res, n_main)` Near the threshold the skewness is sitting right at 0.25, and at B = 100,000 it is only measured to about ±0.008. My rule of taking the first n after which *every* tested n passes keeps one lucky simulation from deciding the answer.
- Theory agrees: the skewness of the mean is 2/√n, which equals 0.25 at n = (2/0.25)² = **64**.
- **n = 30 is not enough.** At n = 30 the skewness is still `r f2(at(30)$skewness)`, and a "95%"
  interval misses `r pct(at(30)$upper_tail)` of the time on the high side but only
  `r pct(at(30)$lower_tail)` on the low side.

## 7. What surprised me?

> My prediction of 45 was too low; the final answer was `r n_main`. At n = 45 the histogram already
> looked normal to me, but the numbers did not agree. The skewness was still `r f2(at(45)$skewness)`,
> and only `r pct(at(45)$lower_tail)` of the means fell below the lower 1.96 SE limit instead of 2.5%.
> I saw the same pattern with the river lengths at n = 30: the histogram looked fine, but the Q-Q plot
> still curved. I learned not to rely on the histogram alone.

## 8. Reproducibility experiment: a different seed

The assignment asks to rerun one analysis with a different seed. I reran the full two-stage search
with seed **2026** instead of `r student_id`.

```{r}
#| label: reproducibility
exper2 <- run_with_refinement(rgen, coarse, mu, sigma, seed = 2026)
res2   <- exper2$results
n_main2 <- smallest_normal_n(res2)
cmp <- data.frame(
  Seed = c(student_id, 2026),
  `Chosen n (main)` = c(n_main, n_main2),
  `Strict n` = c(n_std[["strict"]], n_by_standard(res2)[["strict"]]),
  `Lenient n` = c(n_std[["lenient"]], n_by_standard(res2)[["lenient"]]),
  `Skewness at n = 30` = f3(c(at(30)$skewness, res2$skewness[res2$n == 30])),
  `Skewness at n = 100` = f3(c(at(100)$skewness, res2$skewness[res2$n == 100])),
  check.names = FALSE)
write.csv(cmp, "../results/reproducibility.csv", row.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(cmp, align = "r")
```

**Did the exact results change?** Yes. Every number in the table moved slightly, because a different
seed produces different random samples.

**Did my scientific conclusion change?** No. Both seeds put the threshold in the same narrow range
around the theoretical value of 64, both show that n = 30 is not enough, and both show skewness as the
bottleneck. With B = 100,000 the Monte Carlo noise is small compared with the effects I am measuring.
A seed makes a result **reproducible** (anyone can get exactly my numbers); a large B makes it
**reliable** (the conclusion does not depend on the seed).
